claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be prepared as a simple, homogeneous, single-phase solid solution by solution annealing.
Solution-annealed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
Solution-annealed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high plasticity and machinability.
The homogeneous single-phase solid solution permits facile dislocation motion.
Dynamic recovery through cross-slip and dislocation annihilation occurs during deformation.
Dynamic recovery limits dislocation accumulation and work hardening.
Facile dislocation motion and enhanced dynamic recovery govern the low hardness and strength of the alloy.
At room temperature, dislocations dynamically rearrange through cross-slip and climb.
Room-temperature dislocation rearrangement mitigates the buildup of dislocation density.
Cryogenic temperature reduces atomic mobility and retards dynamic-recovery processes.
Retarding dynamic recovery at cryogenic temperature produces greater dislocation accumulation or pile-up.
Cryogenic testing will produce significantly higher yield strength than room-temperature testing.
Cryogenic testing will produce significantly higher hardness than room-temperature testing.
Cryogenic testing will produce higher work-hardening rates than room-temperature testing.
The cryogenically deformed material will exhibit greater dislocation density and fewer recovery features than the room-temperature-deformed material.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state under quasi-static loading and matched processing histories.
Recovery may not be the sole determinant of strength because inherent lattice softness or local chemical fluctuations may also contribute.
